explanation: This capability is the ability to use metadata-driven inventory and discovery tools to quickly locate, classify, and assess existing data assets across the organization before proposing new collections. It supports more automated, enterprise-wide work by enabling staff to evaluate data availability, concept alignment, reusability, automation readiness, and feasibility using digital platforms, standardized metadata, and documented business case processes.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in GSBPM 1.1, 1.4, and 1.5 requires automated data discovery, metadata-assisted concept identification, and systematic suitability assessment before new surveys or projects are approved, while the current role does not explicitly include these responsibilities. This shift is driven by the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide, which collectively emphasize digital-first operations, enterprise coordination, reuse of existing data assets, automation, and evidence-based decision-making for new data initiatives.

explanation: Automation Readiness and Solution Scoping is the capability to assess whether a data need can be met through automation, reuse of existing assets, or alternative data sources before launching new collection work. It includes using standardized methods to evaluate feasibility, cost, risk, reusability, and strategic fit, and to document business cases that support metadata-driven, interoperable, and digitally enabled collection design across needs identification and collection activities.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future-state work described in the Departmental Plan, Mandate letters, and the StatCan 2030 Future Slide requires staff to identify needs through enterprise-wide, digitally enabled triage rather than defaulting to new surveys. These change drivers increase expectations for formal automation assessment, cost and feasibility modeling, reuse of existing data and instruments, and business case documentation in GSBPM 1.1, 2.3, and 3.1, directly shaping future work toward modular, AI-enabled, and reusable collection solutions.

explanation: This capability is the ability to use enterprise business intelligence, metadata, and digital collaboration tools to assess existing data assets, evaluate feasibility, and model the cost, risk, and value of proposed collections or projects. It supports more solution-oriented work in identifying and confirming needs, where staff must triage requests, compare reuse versus new collection options, and produce evidence-based business cases that align with enterprise standards and rapid digital workflows.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in GSBPM 1.1, 1.2, and 3.1 requires staff to use digital discovery platforms, metadata-driven tools, and formal cost-benefit and risk analysis before proposing new collection instruments. This is directly influenced by the change drivers in Mandate letters, the Departmental Plan, and the StatCan 2030 Future Slide, which emphasize digital transformation, enterprise coordination, reuse of existing data, automation, and stronger evidence-based prioritization for new statistical activities.

explanation: Digital Collaboration & Enterprise Coordination is the capability to use enterprise digital platforms to coordinate cross-functional needs identification, document decisions, and support transparent collaboration across programs. It includes working in shared tools to assess existing data assets, capture feasibility and cost considerations, and build business case documentation that supports automation, auditability, and faster enterprise-wide decision-making.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide point to more integrated, digital, and enterprise-wide ways of working, with stronger expectations for reuse of existing data, automation, and coordinated decision-making. These change drivers directly influence future work in GSBPM 1.1 and 1.2 by requiring digitally enabled consultation, metadata-supported discovery, and formal cost-benefit documentation, and in 7.3 by reinforcing the need to operate through governed enterprise platforms, version-controlled workflows, and coordinated release processes.

explanation: Digital stakeholder engagement is the capability to coordinate consultations, collaboration, and release-related interactions through enterprise digital platforms using structured workflows, asynchronous communication, and searchable documentation. It includes guiding stakeholders through data discovery, formal needs triage, and decision logging, while supporting agile, transparent coordination across consultation, dissemination, and promotion activities.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide all point toward more digital, integrated, and transparent service delivery, stronger partner engagement, and greater use of enterprise platforms, automation, and AI-enabled tools. These change drivers directly influence future work requirements in GSBPM 1.2, 7.3, and 7.4 by requiring staff to manage formal digital consultations, coordinate dissemination through governed platforms, and support metadata-driven, omnichannel engagement with internal and external stakeholders.

explanation: This capability is the ability to assess whether a proposed data initiative is necessary, viable, and aligned with enterprise priorities, then translate that assessment into a clear, evidence-based business case. It requires staff to work across teams using standardized digital tools to triage needs, evaluate existing internal, administrative, and alternative data sources before proposing new collection, and document cost, risk, automation, and strategic fit for governance decisions.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide collectively point to more digital, enterprise-wide, and efficiency-driven ways of working, where new data requests must be formally triaged and justified rather than advanced through program-specific approaches. These change drivers directly influence future work in GSBPM 1.1, 1.5, and 1.6 by requiring solution scoping, automated and metadata-enabled assessment of data availability and suitability, and stronger business cases that demonstrate reuse, automation opportunities, and alignment with enterprise platforms before any new collection is approved.

explanation: This capability is the ability to design and use analytic workflows that are modular, reusable, and automated so processing and dissemination can be delivered efficiently at enterprise scale. It includes selecting approved components, configuring standardized toolkits, managing version-controlled pipelines, and ensuring workflows are auditable, secure, reproducible, and suitable for broad reuse across programs.
justification: This skill gap was selected because Mandate letters, the Departmental Plan, and the StatCan 2030 Future Slide collectively drive more standardized, efficient, and enterprise-wide ways of working, increasing expectations for automation, reuse, and rapid delivery. These change drivers influence future work in GSBPM 1.5, 2.5, and 3.2 by requiring automated data suitability assessment, metadata-driven and template-based design, and modular microservice-based processing components, making reusability and automation essential for analysis and dissemination workflows.

explanation: AI/Automation Platform Familiarity is the capability to use and assess digital platforms that support AI-enabled data discovery, metadata-driven asset inventory, business intelligence, and automated workflow coordination. In practice, it means staff can identify and evaluate existing data sources, scope solution options with cost and risk considerations, and work within enterprise tools that support faster, more standardized needs assessment, concept identification, and data suitability decisions.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide points to more automated, enterprise-wide, and digitally enabled approaches to identifying needs, checking data availability, and identifying concepts. Those change drivers increase the requirement for staff to use AI/automation platforms for metadata-based discovery, suitability screening, cost/risk-informed solution scoping, and coordinated digital workflows—capabilities that are not explicitly covered in current technical activities.

explanation: Platform Navigation and Facilitation is the capability to use data discovery and sharing platforms to guide stakeholders through available data assets, metadata, and suitability assessments, while supporting rapid, collaborative decision-making. In practice, it means facilitating digitally enabled consultations that help confirm needs, assess reuse and fit-for-purpose, and document trade-offs before proposing new collection activities.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide collectively point to more digital, efficient, and reuse-focused service delivery, with stronger expectations for automation, transparency, and evidence-based prioritization. These change drivers directly influence future work in GSBPM 1.1, 1.2, and 1.5 by requiring staff to identify needs through platform-enabled discovery, confirm needs through faster iterative consultations, and assess data availability through metadata-driven tools before considering new surveys.

explanation: Data Asset Evaluation is the capability to work with stakeholders to quickly assess existing data holdings, administrative sources, and alternative data for suitability, quality, legal/privacy considerations, and overall fit-for-purpose before considering new collection. In practice, this means using data discovery platforms, metadata, and structured consultation methods to compare options, support reuse, and document evidence-based decisions during needs identification, needs confirmation, and data availability assessment.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide collectively drive a shift toward digital service delivery, greater reuse of existing data assets, reduced respondent burden, and more efficient, evidence-based decisions about when new data collection is truly necessary. These change drivers directly influence future work in GSBPM 1.1, 1.2, and 1.5 by requiring staff to use automated discovery tools, facilitate rapid iterative consultations, and jointly evaluate existing assets with stakeholders before advancing any survey proposal.

explanation: Outcome-Oriented Engagement is the ability to lead stakeholder consultations toward clear decisions by using prioritization criteria, trade-offs, and explicit reuse-versus-new-collection reasoning. In future needs identification, consultation, and data suitability assessment activities, employees must use metadata and data discovery platforms to jointly assess existing assets, document decisions, and guide stakeholders toward fit-for-purpose, evidence-based options through faster, more iterative engagement.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide all point to a more digital, agile, and reuse-first operating model in which new collection is more tightly justified and decisions must align with strategic priorities, efficiency, and reduced burden. These change drivers directly influence future work in GSBPM 1.1, 1.2, and 1.5 by requiring staff to facilitate platform-enabled consultations, apply cost-benefit and prioritization frameworks, and support transparent decisions on whether existing data can meet needs before proposing new statistical activities.

explanation: Collaborative Asset Assessment is the capability to lead structured sessions with stakeholders to identify, review, and compare existing data assets using discovery platforms, metadata, and suitability criteria before proposing new collection. It requires staff to facilitate trade-off discussions on feasibility, timeliness, quality, cost, and reuse so that needs are met through the best available assets and only complex gaps escalate to new survey design.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in GSBPM 1.1, 1.2, and 1.5 shifts effort from acquiring new data to digitally enabled needs triage, joint asset discovery, and evidence-based suitability assessment of existing holdings, administrative data, and alternative sources. This direction is driven by Mandate letters, the Departmental Plan, and the StatCan 2030 Future Slide, which emphasize modernization, reuse of existing data, reduced response burden, faster decision-making, and transparent prioritization—thereby increasing the need for staff who can facilitate collaborative co-assessment and asset-based decision-making.

explanation: This capability is the ability to apply clear, formal criteria to decide when existing data assets, components, or metadata can be reused and when new collection or development is justified. In practice, it supports faster, more transparent decisions during needs identification, consultation, and component reuse by weighing cost, impact, timeliness, feasibility, respondent burden, and strategic fit, while documenting trade-offs and mitigation strategies for management.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in the Departmental Plan, Mandate letters, and the StatCan 2030 Future Slide shifts project leadership away from defaulting to new acquisition and toward enterprise reuse, digital discovery, automation, and outcome-based prioritization. Across GSBPM 1.1, 1.2, and 3.2, staff will need to use searchable metadata platforms, standardized tools, and explicit cost-benefit and impact frameworks to justify decisions, manage risks, and document why reuse, mitigation, or new collection best meets future operational requirements.

explanation: Automated Consultation Facilitation is the capability to lead stakeholder discussions and negotiations through digital discovery and metadata platforms, using rapid, evidence-based assessment of existing data assets before proposing new collection. It combines platform navigation, data discovery, and facilitation skills so staff can guide iterative consultations, surface trade-offs, and support transparent decisions based on feasibility, timeliness, reuse, and organizational priorities.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in GSBPM 1.1, 1.2, and 1.5 shifts needs identification, consultation, and data suitability assessment toward searchable metadata platforms, automated screening, and faster AI-supported decision cycles. This direction is driven by the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide, which collectively emphasize digital-first service delivery, greater use of existing administrative and alternative data, stronger efficiency and transparency, and more rigorous justification before launching new surveys.

explanation: Digital Stakeholder Collaboration is the capability to use digital platforms, metadata-enabled tools, and collaborative workflows to engage partners, assess needs, and support faster joint decisions. In practice, it includes facilitating consultations through dashboards and discovery platforms, guiding trade-off and cost-benefit discussions, and synthesizing outcomes in ways that are transparent, auditable, and aligned with agile, reusable, and automated ways of working.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future-state work described in GSBPM 1.1, 1.2, and 3.3 requires staff to conduct stakeholder engagement, needs identification, and dissemination design through digital platforms, machine-actionable metadata, and standardized collaborative environments. This aligns with the change drivers in the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide, which collectively emphasize digital service delivery, enterprise reuse, faster decision-making, and AI- and automation-enabled operations, thereby increasing the need for strong digital facilitation, consultation, and outcome-analysis capabilities.

explanation: Digital Workflow Assessment is the capability to judge whether proposed objectives and workflow designs can be delivered effectively within a modular, automated, interoperable production environment. It requires staff to assess feasibility early using enterprise data assets, metadata, reuse options, automation constraints, and cross-team dependencies, while clearly justifying any need for manual processes, bespoke solutions, or new collection.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future-state requirements in the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and Statcan 2030 Future Slide shift work from traditional objective-setting based mainly on statistical value to decisions that must also satisfy digital feasibility, reuse, automation, interoperability, and speed-to-delivery criteria. As reflected in GSBPM 1.1, 1.3, and 2.6, these change drivers require staff to evaluate needs and output objectives against enterprise pipeline architectures, asset reuse expectations, and standardized workflow design from the outset, creating a clear need for stronger digital workflow assessment capability.

explanation: This capability is the ability to apply the agency’s interoperability, automation, and machine-readable standards when defining needs, setting output objectives, and designing reusable dissemination components. It ensures staff can assess digital workflow feasibility early, default to asset reuse and standardized automated solutions, document justified exceptions, and align with enterprise platforms, metadata, APIs, and cross-team delivery requirements from the outset.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide collectively drive work toward reuse-first, digitally enabled, interoperable, and automation-ready operations. Those change drivers directly reshape GSBPM activities 1.1, 1.3, and 3.3 by requiring staff to evaluate existing data assets before new collection, set machine-actionable and automation-compatible objectives, and build dissemination through standardized reusable components, making knowledge of agency standards essential to future work.

explanation: This capability is the ability to build clear, evidence-based objective and business case documentation that shows why a proposed output should proceed, how it will work within enterprise digital workflows, and when exceptions to data reuse or automation are justified. It requires staff to assess feasibility early, document interoperability and automation requirements, and support cross-functional decisions with transparent cost-benefit, risk, and implementation rationale across objective-setting, business case development, and action planning.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in GSBPM 1.3, 1.6, and 8.3 requires stronger upfront justification, documentation, and defence of decisions than traditional output planning. This is driven by the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide, which collectively emphasize reuse of existing data, digital-first and automated delivery, interoperability, faster governance, and measurable accountability—thereby increasing the need for rigorous value cases that justify new collection, manual processes, or non-standard solutions.

explanation: Cross-disciplinary stakeholder engagement is the capability to bring program, IT, digital product, and automation experts together early to set output objectives that are feasible, reusable, and automation-ready. It enables staff to assess digital workflow compatibility, interoperability, metadata, timelines, and asset reuse at the outset, so decisions about new collection, system design, and production approaches are made collaboratively and with clear trade-offs.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future-state requirements in the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide collectively push work toward reuse of existing data, automation-by-default, interoperability, faster delivery, and stronger enterprise-wide collaboration. Those change drivers directly reshape GSBPM 1.2, 1.3, and 2.6 by requiring needs confirmation, objective setting, and workflow design to be jointly informed by IT and digital feasibility, cost-benefit discipline, and cross-team alignment from the beginning rather than later in production.

explanation: Automated Data Integration Planning is the capability to assess data acquisition and integration options early and design approaches that are machine-actionable, interoperable, and ready for automated workflows. It enables leaders to scope projects with clear expectations for metadata, FAIR-aligned standards, reusable integration components, and auditable pipelines so data can be integrated rapidly with minimal manual effort. This shifts work from planning one-off acquisitions or manual integration toward configuring scalable integration rules, validating suitability, and managing exceptions within shared digital platforms.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide collectively drive a more digital, interoperable, and automation-ready operating model, where existing and external data must be assessed and integrated before new collection is pursued. These change drivers influence future work in GSBPM 1.1, 1.5, and 5.1 by requiring solution-oriented needs identification, automated data availability and suitability assessment, and AI-enabled integration through standardized metadata, reusable modules, and auditable orchestration. As a result, leaders must now evaluate automation feasibility and integration pathways at project scoping, making digital operationalization a core requirement rather than a downstream consideration.

explanation: Digital/Automation-Centric Stakeholder Facilitation is the ability to lead consultations and design discussions so partners align early on digital workflows, interoperability standards, metadata requirements, and automation objectives—not just program needs. This capability supports future work in needs confirmation, dissemination, and production system design by helping teams translate technical constraints and opportunities into shared decisions that enable reusable, machine-actionable, and scalable solutions.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the change drivers in the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide point to a future operating model built on digital service delivery, interoperability, reuse, and automation. Those drivers directly influence work in GSBPM 1.2, 2.1, and 2.6 by requiring staff to facilitate stakeholder discussions that confirm needs through metadata-enabled platforms, design outputs for API-based and machine-actionable dissemination, and secure agreement on modular, auditable, automation-first workflows across business and IT boundaries.

explanation: Automated Data Discovery Tool Proficiency is the capability to use automated platforms that scan, assess, and prioritize internal, administrative, alternative, and external data sources, while validating outputs and intervening when complex exceptions arise. As work shifts from manual source checking and processing design to oversight of automated, metadata-driven workflows, staff must be able to monitor system results, troubleshoot issues, and apply judgment in non-routine legal, privacy, quality, and partner negotiation cases.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in the StatCan 2030 Future Slide for GSBPM 1.1, 1.5, and 2.5 requires staff to rely on automated discovery, suitability screening, and machine-actionable workflow design rather than manual data acquisition and assessment. It is further driven by priorities reflected in Mandate letters and the Departmental Plan to modernize operations, increase automation, strengthen use of administrative and alternative data, and ensure secure, auditable, and efficient decision-making—making proficiency with automated acquisition tools essential for meeting future operational requirements.

skill_gap: Advanced Data Privacy and Legal Risk Assessment
explanation: Advanced Data Privacy and Legal Risk Assessment is the capability to evaluate new, alternative, or sensitive data sources against legal, privacy, ethical, and disclosure requirements before they are acquired or integrated into automated statistical workflows. As data discovery, suitability screening, and processing design become more automated across needs identification, source assessment, and workflow configuration, staff must focus on complex exceptions, non-routine negotiations, and high-risk decisions that require expert judgment.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in the Departmental Plan and the StatCan 2030 Future Slide shifts effort away from routine manual assessment toward automated discovery, metadata-driven suitability screening, and reusable processing pipelines, leaving staff to manage edge cases involving novel data, sensitive information, and complex legal/privacy risks. It is also reinforced by Mandate letter expectations for responsible, trusted use of data and digital modernization, which increase the need for specialists who can assess legal and ethical implications, support evidence-based decisions on whether new collection is necessary, and enable compliant integration of new data sources into automated operations.

explanation: Strategic Data Partnership Management is the capability to build, negotiate, and sustain high-value relationships with non-traditional data providers so the organization can access emerging data assets in a compliant, reliable, and reusable way. As data discovery, suitability screening, and routine integration become increasingly automated across needs consultation, source assessment, and data integration activities, employees will need to focus more on complex partner engagement, legal and ethical risk management, metadata expectations, and long-term partnership innovation.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide all point toward greater use of administrative, alternative, and private-sector data, stronger modernization of data acquisition, and more automated, interoperable production processes. Those change drivers shift future work in GSBPM 1.2, 1.5, and 5.1 away from routine outreach and manual integration toward complex negotiation with new data holders, compliance oversight, and strategic relationship management to secure data that automated systems can discover, assess, and integrate.

explanation: Machine-actionable metadata structures are the standardized metadata frameworks that allow systems to automatically discover, assess, integrate, and govern data with minimal manual intervention. This capability supports faster concept identification, automated data availability and suitability checks, and auditable data integration by ensuring data assets are structured for interoperability, FAIR use, and compliance. It also enables specialists to focus on complex exceptions, legal and ethical considerations, and strategic partner engagement rather than routine manual processing.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in the Departmental Plan, Mandate letters, and the StatCan 2030 Future Slide points to greater automation, expanded use of administrative and alternative data, and stronger expectations for interoperable, compliant, and reusable data assets. These change drivers directly influence GSBPM activities 1.4, 1.5, and 5.1 by requiring machine-actionable metadata to support automated concept alignment, suitability screening, and integration workflows, while enabling specialists to manage emerging partnerships with new data providers and ensure legal, privacy, and governance requirements are met.

skill_gap: Advanced Negotiation Techniques for Data Acquisition
explanation: This capability is the ability to negotiate access to complex, sensitive, or proprietary data in situations where standard agreements are not sufficient. It includes securing terms on privacy, access, usage, and disclosure while working with legal, privacy, methodological, and technical experts to support automated data discovery, evidence-based source selection, and integration of new data into standardized processing environments.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide all point toward greater use of administrative, alternative, and partner-held data, stronger privacy and stewardship expectations, and more automated, metadata-driven decisions about whether existing data can replace new collection. As work in GSBPM 1.2, 1.5, and 2.5 shifts human effort toward edge cases, high-risk assessments, and relationship management with new data partners, staff need advanced negotiation techniques to secure novel or sensitive data under terms that enable lawful access, reuse, interoperability, and operational integration.

explanation: Automation Oversight and Quality Assurance is the capability to supervise automated validation and analytics processes, assess whether outputs are accurate, trustworthy, and auditable, and investigate anomalies or edge cases that automation cannot resolve on its own. As work shifts away from manual integration and review, specialists must monitor metadata-driven pipelines, interpret flagged exceptions, refine validation rules, and ensure automated outputs meet quality, transparency, and ethical standards across validation and interpretation activities.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future work described in the Departmental Plan, Mandate letters, and the StatCan 2030 Future Slide points to greater use of automation, AI-enabled validation, and standardized auditable pipelines, which changes the role from hands-on processing to oversight, exception management, and assurance. The change drivers directly influence activities such as reviewing and validating inputs, validating outputs, and interpreting results by requiring staff to oversee automated rules, diagnose anomalies, maintain trust in AI-supported processes, and remain accountable for final data quality in faster, more automated workflows.

explanation: This capability is the ability to configure, monitor, and troubleshoot automated data workflows built on standardized, modular, and auditable platforms, including low-code/no-code and event-driven tools. It requires staff to shift from performing manual processing tasks to managing reusable workflow components, applying version control and governance practices, and stepping in when automation encounters exceptions, new requirements, or failures. The capability also supports closer collaboration between business and IT to maintain reliable, scalable, and compliant production systems.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the change drivers in the Mandate letters, Departmental Plan, and StatCan 2030 Future Slide point to a future operating model centered on automation, interoperability, auditability, and faster adaptation of statistical production. Those drivers directly influence future work in GSBPM 3.4, 2.6, and 2.5 by shifting responsibilities from manual handling and custom one-off processes toward configuring modular workflows, embedding machine-actionable rules and metadata, and troubleshooting automated systems within enterprise guardrails.

explanation: Enterprise Registry Protocols is the capability to use enterprise metadata registries, variable standards, and governance rules so variables are defined, documented, versioned, and reused consistently across programs. In future work, this supports automated data integration, derivation, and interoperability by shifting effort away from manual reconciliation toward registry-based stewardship, metadata quality assurance, and standards-driven design.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the future state described in the Departmental Plan and the StatCan 2030 Future Slide requires metadata-driven, interoperable, and automated production processes across variable design, data integration, and derivation activities. It is also reinforced by Mandate letters emphasizing modernization, digital service delivery, and better use of data, which together increase the need for staff to apply enterprise registry protocols so variables can be governed, reused, and ingested through standardized, auditable pipelines.

explanation: Interoperability Protocols is the capability to design and validate variables, metadata structures, and API-ready schemas so data can move reliably across systems and be reused in automated workflows. As work in data integration, variable design, and processing becomes more metadata-driven and standardized, specialists will need to ensure variables align with enterprise registries, support FAIR principles, and enable auditable, reusable, machine-actionable pipelines rather than manual reconciliation.
justification: This skill gap was selected because the Departmental Plan and the StatCan 2030 Future Slide point to future work built on interoperable, automated, and reusable data pipelines, while Mandate letters reinforce the need for modern digital service delivery, data sharing, and efficient enterprise operations. These change drivers directly influence GSBPM activities 5.1, 2.2, and 2.5 by shifting requirements toward registry-based stewardship, standardized metadata, API-enabled integration, and configurable processing rules, making interoperability protocols essential for future performance.
